SONiC · VRF rehome · sonic-buildimage #27608 · #28619 · #29919 · VRF bind guard HLD (pinned at 56a88d8)

The rehoming bench

Moving a SONiC interface into another VRF can leave its hardware behind in the old one. Three reported failures, one narrow fix and the proposed VRF bind guard, replayed on one machine.

In one minute. In SONiC an interface lives twice. Linux knows which VRF the interface belongs to. orchagent separately owns a hardware router interface (RIF), and the RIF's virtual router is fixed when it is created. So a VRF move needs a new RIF, and the old RIF can only be removed once nothing references it any more: no route, neighbor, next hop or next-hop group.

There is a window when Linux has already moved but the old RIF is still in place. Any new work that reaches orchagent in that window can attach to the old RIF. A route can be programmed in the new VRF on a RIF that still belongs to the old one, so traffic is looked up in the wrong VRF. Or new references can pin the old RIF so it never retires.

The proposed bind guard makes orchagent confirm a guard before Linux moves. While the guard is up, new references wait and cleanup goes on. The old RIF retires before the new one is created, and the guard comes down only after that retirement.

    How to read the machine

    The figure is one machine shown from one camera, and every replay below runs on it. Switching the fit-out (before #4645, the narrow fix, the bind guard) only pins or unpins linkages that are always there. Switching the sequence only changes the starting state and the order in which work arrives. Parts that a fit-out does not use stay in place, greyed and inert.

    • Back: the Linux deck. The binding lever is the interface's Linux VRF membership (ip link set … master / nomaster). The config card is what the operator asked for in CONFIG_DB; the recorded-state card is IntfMgr's STATE_DB record. The route dispenser (kernel → zebra → fpmsyncd) and the neighbor dispenser (kernel → neighsyncd) release work when Linux changes.
    • Middle: chutes and stations. Each chute is an APPL_DB table. Work lands in the in-tray of its consumer: IntfsOrch, RouteOrch or NeighOrch. One service carriage on the gantry is orchagent's single-threaded event loop. It runs one consumer at a time, and the order it visits them in is the order work is processed.
    • Front: the RIF seat. The RIF plate's hue and tab show the virtual router it was created in (graphite = default VR, blue = VrfBlue VR, red = VrfRed VR). Its rim notches tell RIFs apart. A peg pushed into the plate is a new reference; the dial counts them. The hoist can only lift a plate that no peg pins. The press stamps a new plate and can only feed an empty seat.
    • Fixes. The narrow gate (#4645) sits on the connected-route track only and is worked by IntfsOrch's removal-pending flag. The guard visor (HLD) drops over the back of the seat, where every track arrives. Tall acquisition work cannot pass under it; flat withdrawal discs can.
    • Consequence. A packet ball enters the port and leaves through the window of the plate's virtual router. It lands in the CPU cup (delivered) or falls into a pit (dropped by a blackhole route).

    Glossary

    TermMeaning on this page
    Linux bindingThe kernel VRF membership of the interface: master <vrf> or nomaster (default VRF). Changed by IntfMgr.
    RIF (router interface)orchagent's SAI object for the interface. Its virtual router (VR) is set when it is created, so changing VRF needs a new RIF.
    old RIF / new RIFThe RIF of the interface's previous lifecycle / of the lifecycle the VRF change starts.
    reference, ref_countA dependent object that keeps a RIF in use. A connected route adds one; a neighbor adds one and its next hop another. Routes through an IP next hop, and next-hop groups of IP next hops, hold the next hop (which holds the RIF) rather than the RIF itself. removeRouterIntfs refuses while the count is above zero.
    connected routeA route whose next hop is the interface itself (an interface next hop). RouteOrch programs it on whatever RIF the port has at that moment.
    removal-pending flagm_removingIntfses: IntfsOrch marks an interface after it has tried to remove it and failed. It keeps retrying the removal.
    narrow fixsonic-swss#4645: RouteOrch defers a connected route while isIntfChangeInProgress() (the removal-pending flag) is set.
    bind guard (guard)The HLD's per-interface guard. It is activated and confirmed before the Linux binding changes and released only after the old RIF retires.
    prepare / applied / cancelThe request actions IntfMgr publishes on INTF_GUARD_TABLE, each with a request ID.
    guarded / retired / releasedIntfsOrch's acknowledgment states: guard active; old interface retired but guard still active; guard inactive.
    retirement“Check and retire any old interface”: ports ready → remove old neighbors → remove remaining old prefixes → proxy-ARP cleanup → remove the old RIF.
    retirement obligationRetirement that is still owed, recorded as applied_id ahead of retired_id.
    withdrawal / cleanupWork that releases references (route, neighbor, next-hop-group removal). The guard never blocks it.
    queued for retryWork that cannot run yet. Its owner keeps it, does not program it, and does not count it as processed.
    earlier-arrival race#28619: a route for the new VRF is processed before IntfsOrch has observed the interface transition.

    The reports name the target VRF Vrf01 and the interface PortChannel101. The HLD's examples use VrfBlue and Ethernet0. The machine always calls the target VRF VrfBlue and the old named VRF in the lifecycles VrfRed.

    Three failures, one machine

    1 · sonic-buildimage #27608: the late route closed after #4645

    Reported by Hemanth Kumar Tirupati (NVIDIA), 2026-05-29. Closed 2026-07-24 when sonic-swss#4645 merged; the fix was cherry-picked to 202605 in #4803.

    • Trigger. On a PortChannel with IPv4 and IPv6 BGP neighbors, the IPv4 address is removed and config interface vrf bind PortChannel101 Vrf01 runs while neighbor, next-hop and next-hop-group objects still reference the old RIF. Then the IPv4 address is re-added before the old RIF is gone.
    • Event order. IntfsOrch processes the interface removal first. removeRouterIntfs refuses (“still referenced with ref count 2”), so the removal-pending flag goes up and the removal is retried. Later, the re-added address's Vrf01 connected route reaches RouteOrch. RouteOrch asks for the interface's RIF, gets the old one, and programs the route.
    • Bad state. A route in the Vrf01 virtual router whose next hop is a RIF in the default virtual router. That route is one more reference, so after the neighbors drain the old RIF is still pinned (“ref count 1” in the report).
    • Consequence. Packets entering the interface are looked up in the default VRF. The DHCP OFFER to the Loopback0 address in Vrf01 was dropped as “Blackhole route”.

    2 · sonic-buildimage #28619: the early route open

    Raised by Bojun Feng on 2026-07-25 to track the corner case that #4645's own description names as its limitation. Reproduced in CI by the draft regression test sonic-mgmt#26725. A contributor later reported the same race on physical hardware, on a 202605 image that already includes #4645.

    • Trigger. The same rehome, but the new-VRF connected route reaches RouteOrch before IntfsOrch has observed the interface transition. Per the issue thread, an addressless interface and IPv6 link-local neighbors widen the window; removing link-local neighbors delays the interface path.
    • Event order. RouteOrch runs first. The removal-pending flag is down because IntfsOrch has not even tried the removal yet. So #4645's check reads false, the old RIF is still the interface's RIF, and the route is programmed. IntfsOrch observes the transition afterwards; its removal now fails, partly because of the route it never saw.
    • Bad state. The same route/RIF mismatch as #27608, reached by a path the narrow gate never sees.
    • Why retry cannot repair it. Retry only re-runs work that was refused and kept. This route was accepted: nothing is left in RouteOrch's retry rack, and nothing re-checks routes that are already programmed. The flag rises after the gate has let the route through.

    3 · sonic-buildimage #29919: the neighbor path open

    Reported by Hemanth Kumar Tirupati (NVIDIA), 2026-10-02, as a follow-up to #27608 and #4645.

    • Trigger. The old RIF's removal is pending, and #4645 correctly defers the connected route. Then config route add prefix vrf Vrf01 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop vrf Vrf01 10.0.0.57 is applied while the removal is still pending.
    • Event order. The route needs next hop 10.0.0.57, so the neighbor is resolved. NeighOrch::addNeighbor and addNextHop look up the interface's RIF, get the old one, and create the neighbor and next hop on it. That path never passes the narrow gate.
    • Bad state. No mismatched connected route this time. Two new references (neighbor and next hop) pin the old RIF at “ref count 2”, so it never retires, the new RIF is never created, and the connected route waits forever.
    • Consequence. Ingress on PortChannel101 still uses the default VRF and the OFFER never reaches Vrf01. In the report, deleting the default route released the neighbor and next hop and let the rehome finish.

    The shared hole, and why the narrow fix covers one corner of it

    All three are the same hole: new work can acquire a reference to the old RIF after the Linux binding has moved and before the old RIF has retired. They differ in which path the work takes and when it arrives:

    PathWhen IntfsOrch's flag is checkedWhat pins the old RIF#4645
    #27608connected route → RouteOrchflag already upa mismatched route (+1)stops it fixed
    #28619connected route → RouteOrchflag not up yeta mismatched route (+1)reads false open
    #29919neighbor + next hop → NeighOrchnever checked on this pathneighbor and next hop (+2)not on the path open

    The narrow fix is a check placed after the transition becomes visible to IntfsOrch, on one path. A check made only after the transition is visible is too late for work that arrives earlier. The Linux binding moves first, and the kernel can turn that into a route on a path (zebra → fpmsyncd → ROUTE_TABLE) that has no ordering with IntfMgr's INTF_TABLE update. orchagent then runs whichever consumer is ready (OrchDaemon::start). The guard moves the boundary before the Linux change, so nothing the change causes can arrive first.

    Why not just compare VRFs? An early version of #4645 also refused a connected route whose VRF differed from its RIF's VR. That check was removed after review: “This check is not valid. It would break VPN decap, VRF leafing case. We can't assume route vrf would be the same as outgoing port Vrf.” Cross-VRF forwarding is legitimate, so the guard is a lifecycle fence, not a VRF-equality rule. #29919 asks for the same.
    Why not detect and repair afterwards? In #28619 the author reports trying it. When RIF removal is blocked, the reference count records only the end state. It does not say which objects hold the references or what intent created them, and some holders cannot be safely evicted and replayed.

    The bind guard, for newcomers intended design (HLD)

    The HLD (pinned revision 56a88d8, rev 0.1, under review as SONiC#2572, with a draft implementation in sonic-swss#4945) keeps the CLI and CONFIG_DB API unchanged. It adds two ordering rules:

    1. Confirmation before the Linux binding change. IntfMgr asks IntfsOrch to activate the guard and changes the Linux binding only after a matching acknowledgment (guarded or retired).
    2. Retirement before new RIF creation. The new RIF is created only after IntfsOrch has checked and retired any old interface and released the guard.

    While the guard is active, three rules hold:

    • IntfsOrch keeps interface-level and interface-prefix SETs queued.
    • Dependency owners (RouteOrch, NeighOrch, next-hop-group owners) check the guard before creating or reusing objects, including cached neighbors, next hops and next-hop groups. Blocked work stays with its owner: it is neither programmed nor counted as processed.
    • The guard blocks new references, not cleanup lookups. Withdrawal paths still find the old RIF and release what they hold.

    Request and acknowledgment

    RecordWritten byContents
    APPL_DB INTF_GUARD_TABLE:<alias> (guard chute)IntfMgrid, action = prepare · applied · cancel
    STATE_DB INTERFACE_GUARD_TABLE|<alias> (record board)IntfMgrrequest_id, action, target_vrf, kernel_pending, applied_id, applied_vrf
    IntfsOrchacknowledgment id and state = guarded · retired · released; retired_id
    STATE_DB notification INTF_GUARD_ACK (bell)IntfsOrchwakes IntfMgr; the retained record carries the ID and state
    • IntfMgr keeps one current request per interface alias. It allocates a monotonically increasing request_id and persists the request before publishing it. IntfsOrch validates every notification's ID and action against that record, so stale notifications cannot act on a new RIF.
    • prepare = “ask IntfsOrch to activate the guard”. applied = “the Linux binding changed”: IntfMgr records applied_id and applied_vrf, and IntfsOrch then completes retirement and releases the guard for the current request. cancel ends a prepare that never changed the Linux binding.
    • A replacement request takes over the active guard without a gap. No new work can slip in between requests.
    • kernel_pending is set before a guarded Linux binding change and cleared after the recorded interface state is updated. Unfinished Linux binding work therefore stays guarded if processing is interrupted.
    Timeouts retry, they never release. INTF_GUARD_ACK prompts IntfMgr to retry pending work. IntfMgr also retries on a timeout and after other events, so progress never depends on one notification. On the machine, the retry clock only makes IntfMgr re-read the board. The guard's release latch is held by the obligation tag, and only completed retirement removes the tag.

    Retirement, and why cleanup must keep running

    Retirement can only finish when the old RIF's references are gone, and those references are released by withdrawals. If the guard also blocked withdrawals, retirement could never finish, the guard could never be released, and the new RIF would never exist. That is why the visor's edge stops tall acquisition work but lets flat withdrawal discs through.

    IntfsOrch's retirement also asks NeighOrch to remove old neighbors, releasing their RIF references. Existing reference accounting still decides when each step can finish: a neighbor whose next hop is held by a route or a group waits until that holder is withdrawn. BIND and UNBIND do not withdraw anyone's routes; owners withdraw independently. When an attempt is blocked, retirement stays queued and the guard stays active. After old neighbors are removed, NeighOrch requeues a still-desired neighbor SET (if no newer SET or DEL is pending), so it is replayed onto the new RIF.

    Retirement is retained apart from the ordinary interface queue. If an interface DEL and a later SET coalesce, applied_id still records the obligation. IntfsOrch compares applied_id with retired_id to decide whether retirement is unfinished, including when a newer prepare is canceled.

    Lifecycles intended design (HLD)

    UNBIND

    The interface leaves VrfRed and no BIND follows. IntfMgr removes the addresses (IPv6 link-local addresses are not counted). It confirms that the guard is active, detaches the Linux interface, publishes the old interface's removal, reports applied with an empty applied_vrf, and removes the recorded state. IntfsOrch retires the old interface asynchronously. Here a route through the old neighbor pins it until FRR withdraws that route, and new route work through the same neighbor waits under the guard. Then IntfsOrch releases the guard. UNBIND needs no later BIND.

    Clean BIND

    The interface starts detached with no old RIF. The CLI saves the new entry once the old recorded state is gone; it never waits for an old RIF. IntfMgr checks that the interface and VrfBlue are ready, then asks for the guard. Once confirmed, it attaches the Linux interface to VrfBlue and reports applied. The retirement check still runs and finds nothing, the guard is released, and only then is the new RIF created. Addresses and neighbors are supplied independently.

    BIND while an earlier UNBIND's retirement is pending

    The Linux interface is detached and the guard is still active, because the earlier UNBIND's old RIF (VrfRed) is pinned (in the replay, applied_id 7 and retired_id 6). A BIND to VrfBlue takes over the active guard without a gap and attaches the Linux interface. The old objects still belong to the earlier UNBIND, though. They must retire before the guard is released for the new request and before the VrfBlue RIF is created.

    Restart and retained state

    The HLD's recovery claim is narrow, and this page claims no more. With retained database state, IntfsOrch reconstructs active requests and terminal records during startup, before dependency work can use a RIF. IntfMgr reconciles retained prepares and unfinished Linux binding work with configuration and recorded state. It resumes a retained removal before processing a replacement request for a different VRF. That recovery scope assumes the retained request state is available.
